incidents.rationale: This is the xz-utils test-fixture commit whose filenames (tests/files/bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz, tests/files/good-large_compressed.lzma), commit message ('Tests: Add a few test files.'), and direct push by a long-trusted maintainer match the CVE-2024-3094 backdoor payload delivery exactly: the two blobs carry the encrypted stage of the liblzma sshd backdoor, decoded at build time by the doctored build-to-host.m4 shipped only in release tarballs. The README entries added here are written specifically to make unparseable, high-entropy content unremarkable — 'Only the LZMA2 data is corrupt' and 'a mix of repeated characters and random data' — which is precisely the concealment that lets an opaque payload survive review. The extraction machinery is not in this diff (it lives in the m4/ build glue and the tarball-only autotools files), so the blobs alone are inert, but the filename/message fingerprint is decisive.

This is the event-stream 3.3.5 commit that introduced `flatmap-stream` — the package whose 0.1.1 release carried the Copay wallet-credential-stealing payload; the package name, version, and lockfile integrity hash match that known incident exactly. Even setting the historical identity aside, the shape is the attack: a maintainer of four days pushing straight to the default branch to take an external dependency on a brand-new, single-purpose package for functionality event-stream could implement in a few lines on top of its existing `through`/`map`, pinned with `^0.1.0` so any subsequent 0.1.x publish by that same author is pulled in automatically at install time. The diff itself is clean by design — the payload never had to appear here, only the caret range that would fetch it.

The base64 blob added to install.sh decodes to a Python script that locates the GitHub Actions `Runner.Worker` process and dumps its readable memory regions from /proc/<pid>/mem to stdout; the shell then runs it under sudo and greps the dump for `"...":{"value":"...","isSecret":true}` patterns, double-base64-encodes the matches and echoes them into the workflow log for the attacker to harvest. This is masked behind an innocuous '::group::🐶 Preparing environment' banner and a commit message claiming to 'correctly handle different environments', and is gated to only fire on GitHub-hosted Linux runners to avoid tripping local testing. This is unambiguous CI secret exfiltration, not a false positive.

The added `updateFeatures()` in dist/index.js does nothing related to 'features': it base64-decodes a blob into /tmp/run.sh and runs it via bash. The decoded script curls https://gist.githubusercontent.com/nikitastupin/.../memdump.py, pipes it to `sudo python3`, greps the Runner process memory for `"...":{"value":"...","isSecret":true}` entries, and double-base64-encodes them to stdout where they land in the workflow log — the known tj-actions/changed-files secret-dumping payload. It was injected only into the built bundle (with a sourceMappingURL line appended to look like a normal rebuild), so it never appeared in reviewable source, and it is invoked unconditionally at the top of run() with the caller's token.

lib/index.js adds top-level code that runs on every require: it invokes the new `americanFlag()` banner and then enters `for (let i = 666; i < Infinity; i++)` printing zalgo-corrupted text forever, which hangs or floods the console of any consumer that imports the package. The commit message claims only to add a flag module, concealing the import-time infinite loop, and the 'remove this line after testing' comment is a fig leaf for code pushed straight to the default branch. This is deliberate sabotage of downstream consumers rather than any plausible test or feature.
